title: The 10-Year Test for Durable Schools
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio closes a three-part series on school success by asking what would predict that a currently high-performing school will still be succeeding in ten years. He starts from the premise that superintendent changes, staff turnover, board elections and funding shifts are standard operating conditions rather than disruptions, so test scores alone say little about durability. His thought exercise offers several signals: whether a diligent new teacher could succeed through structured curriculum and a strong transmitted culture, whether normal performance demands unsustainable adult effort, whether leaders can name initiatives they declined, and whether bench strength exists beyond one founder. He treats governance as the least controllable factor, since boards reward visible change over continuity. The conclusion is that long-term success is unlikely by accident, and that the schools worth studying are those built to withstand the forces that normally erode them.
points: Turnover, board changes and reform cycles are the normal operating conditions of public education, so the real test of a school is whether its success can survive them.

A durable school is one where a diligent new teacher could walk in and succeed, thanks to structured curriculum, shared materials and a visible, transmitted culture, as Success Academy and Houston’s NES schools illustrate.
Results that depend on superhuman adult effort mask institutional strain, because schools that rely on brilliance or burnout eventually run out of both.
Durable schools have an institutional immune system, the ability to say no to initiatives, and bench strength beyond a single charismatic leader.
Governance is the most underestimated factor, since boards reward visible change over quiet stewardship and rarely hire a superintendent to keep doing what works.
quotes: The instructional model and adult culture, consistent across dozens of schools, were designed on the assumption that ordinary teachers, properly trained and supported, could produce extraordinary outcomes. As noted previously, Success Academy stays aloft despite extremely high teacher turnover. So far, its school prove that durability can coexist with high teacher turnover so long as institutional structures and culture are strong.
What Houston appears to be doing is not assuming that great teaching will happen; they’re engineering conditions that make competent teaching unavoidable.

Some schools produce impressive gains because teachers work unsustainable hours, constantly design their own materials, and carry enormous instructional loads. For a time, this can look like institutional excellence, but often it masks institutional strain: schools that depend on brilliance or burnout eventually run out of both.

I’d feel particularly confident I was in a school whose success was likely to endure if its team could name initiatives they declined. Stability in education rarely comes from discovering the perfect program; it comes from protecting the ones that already work. From the outside, this may look and sound unimaginative, but schools rarely fail because they lack ideas. They fail because they adopt too many.
